headline: Total remuneration packages offered by 45% of NZ employers risk undermining KiwiSaver integrity as mandatory contribution rates rise
reasoning: Matt McPherson highlights that nearly half of New Zealand employers offer total remuneration packages, which can effectively mean employer KiwiSaver contributions come out of the employee's own salary rather than being additive. He warns this risks shortchanging employees and undermining the integrity of KiwiSaver, particularly as mandated contribution levels increase. He calls on employers to review these arrangements and consider whether they genuinely serve employees' and the country's best interests.
quote: Employers, if you're one of the 45% of employers that offer total rent packages, you go away and make sure you're not shortchanging your staff as compulsory contribution levels go up. I'd also like to encourage you to think about whether it's in the best interests of your people and your company and the country as a whole because I've failed to be convinced that it is.
episode_title: Are kids the key to a better KiwiSaver?

headline: Australian superannuation system amplifies wealth inequality rather than reducing it, warns Sharesies KiwiSaver head
reasoning: Matt McPherson and Max Rashbrook both caution against New Zealand uncritically adopting the Australian superannuation model. While Australia's system has real strengths in aggregate savings levels, it amplifies disparities from working-age income differences. The 12% compulsory contribution rate is applied to very different income bases, and Australia also provides tax breaks for saving that disproportionately benefit higher earners. New Zealand's retirement commission has noted that NZ's system actually diminishes working-age disparities, whereas Australia's amplifies them.
quote: Look, it's got some real strengths. But we're all very aware now just how much more they're saving than we are. And that's great. But yeah, it does. Our retirement commission said, the good thing about New Zealand's retirement system is it diminishes the disparities between people in working age years. The Australian system amplifies those disparities. And that's partly as you say, because people are saving 12% of very different incomes. It's also because Australia provides tax breaks for saving. And that's one of those ideas that sounds intuitively great. And you can think about the fact that the people who will take most advantage of that are the people who are able to save the most. So it's quite regressive.
episode_title: Are kids the key to a better KiwiSaver?

headline: Speaker notes Australia's larger economy and wealth base makes it an easy but not straightforward comparison for New Zealanders considering emigration
reasoning: The speaker cautions against directly comparing New Zealand to Australia, noting that Australia operates a fundamentally different economy with substantially more wealth. Queensland alone has roughly the same population as all of New Zealand. The speaker suggests New Zealanders look overseas and expect equivalent scale and development, without accounting for the volume difference.
quote: I just don't think you're comparing New Zealand to Australia because without losing an hour to it, they do completely different things in their economy. They have a lot more wealth. They may be behind on other things that we're ahead of, and they, maybe three hours away, but I think there's five million people in Brisbane or Queensland alone. Well, that's roughly our population of our entire country. So I think we do look overseas and think we should have everything, and it should be amazing and should look like that. But forget, maybe we don't have that volume.
episode_title: Bite: Should ambitious Gen Z leave New Zealand? (Bonus)

headline: Speaker recently invested capital into a New Zealand tech startup as part of a thesis to support local ecosystem development
reasoning: The speaker shares a personal thesis that once individuals move beyond financial survival mode, they should deploy resources — capital and connections — to support causes and ventures they care about. He recently invested in a tech startup because early-stage companies need both capital and networks. He draws on his own experience of having received similar support and sees paying it forward as a way to contribute to New Zealand's economy.
quote: I recently invested into a tech startup. Yeah, because that's what they need at the moment. They need connection and they need capital. And many years ago, people gave me those things. I was given capital and I was given connections and still am. And I think, okay, well, like someone did this for me, I can do it for someone else.
episode_title: Bite: Should ambitious Gen Z leave New Zealand? (Bonus)

headline: AI adoption lagging among New Zealand SMEs relative to Asia-Pacific peers
reasoning: CPA Australia data cited by Kemeys shows only one in four New Zealand SME owners believe technology investment will improve profitability. By contrast, Asia-Pacific peers are prioritising AI investment. Kemeys attributes NZ's lag partly to an older business-owner demographic, with businesses run by under-40s being three times more likely to be growing.
quote: When Kiwi business owners and the SME space think about investing in technology, only one in four of them think that it will improve their product profitability and probably therefore maybe productivity as well.
episode_title: Can you still hit your first $100k? With Luke Kemeys of Keep the Change

headline: S&P 500 back to all-time highs but potential complacency flagged amid AI-driven rally
reasoning: Kemeys notes the S&P 500 has recovered to all-time highs and that investors seem unfazed by recent volatility. He flags concern that markets may be getting complacent, drawing parallels to end-of-2020 AI bubble commentary. However, he acknowledges a key difference from prior bubbles: today's most highly valued companies are also the most profitable, which he views as a more rational market dynamic.
quote: I was pretty shocked that the S&P 500 for instance is back to all-time highs and people don't seem to be too phased about the volatility whether maybe I'm a little bit worried we're getting a little bit complacent about just how you know, maybe how bubbly it could be.
episode_title: Can you still hit your first $100k? With Luke Kemeys of Keep the Change

headline: New Zealand's kiwifruit industry described as a multi-decade economic phenomenon with $4.5bn in export sales and strong grower returns
reasoning: The kiwifruit industry has generated NZD $4.5 billion in export sales and employs tens of thousands, with positive and profitable returns to growers and investors sustained over 15–20 years. The product's nutritional profile, clean-green credentials and safe production standards underpin global consumer demand. The industry is described as a genuine economic phenomenon for New Zealand.
quote: Kiwi Fruit is an economic phenomena for New Zealand. Four and a half billion dollars in export sales. Tens of thousands of people employed. Positive and very profitable returns going back to growers and investors.
episode_title: Bite: Inside NZ's billion-dollar kiwifruit industry

headline: Seeka's diversification into avocados and Australian fresh produce provides theoretical resilience but kiwifruit growth continues to dominate the business
reasoning: Following the PSA vine disease crisis in 2010, Seeka strategically diversified into avocados and Australian fresh produce (Seeka Fresh) to reduce kiwifruit dependency. However, the strong rebound and continued growth in kiwifruit has dwarfed the contribution of these newer divisions. Management believes the diversification strategy remains sound over the long term.
quote: The issue that's happened to us is that when PSA came in 2010, we were brought to our knees because of our dependence on Kiwi Fruit. So then we decided strategically there that we wanted to add bits into the company... Kiwi Fruit went boof and like, and any growth we had in other places has been swamped and dwarfed by the growth in Kiwi Fruit.
episode_title: Bite: Inside NZ's billion-dollar kiwifruit industry

headline: India Free Trade Agreement opens a new market channel for NZ kiwifruit, potentially boosting Zespri volumes and grower returns
reasoning: High tariffs have historically constrained kiwifruit sales into India. The newly announced FTA removes this barrier, giving Zespri the opportunity to improve returns from existing Indian sales and expand volumes, providing a diversification buffer if other major markets face geopolitical or economic headwinds.
quote: What it does is it gives Zespri the potential for another market to be added to its mix because at the moment we're paying high tariffs in that market.

headline: Seeka CEO outlines growth trajectory, automation strategy and diversification for the NZ-listed horticulture services company
reasoning: Seeka, the second-largest post-harvest provider in New Zealand's kiwifruit sector with ~20% market share, has grown revenues from $30m to $440m. The CEO highlights ongoing automation and AI-driven cool-store logistics as key margin levers, while geographic diversification into Australia and new fruit varieties (including persimmons, avocados, citrus) reduce single-crop dependency. The company expects continued volume growth as Zespri releases new varieties and more orchards come into production, and sees the India Free Trade Agreement as a potential new demand channel.
quote: We are automating, we are innovating, we have brought some new technology to the industry this year to remove labour and to make us faster, better, smarter. And that's the game that we play.

headline: Climate change is an immediate and present risk for outdoor horticulture, requiring active adaptation in rootstock and variety selection
reasoning: The CEO notes that climate change is already affecting growing conditions, with increased rainfall and altered chilling requirements. Seeka is adapting through new rootstock tolerant to high water levels and varieties requiring less wind-chill, but weather events remain an uncontrollable risk for any company growing fruit outdoors.
quote: Climate change is real. It's not something that's going to come. It's something that is here now.

headline: Significant inflationary pressure on electricity and packaging costs poses a headwind to NZ horticulture operators
reasoning: Seeka uses 45 gigawatts of power annually to run its cool stores, and electricity costs are rising sharply. Packaging costs are also increasing, forcing the company to pass costs on to growers. Solar generation offsets some demand but is seasonal, and load management technology is expected to reduce power demand by only 5-10%.
quote: We are in a period of significant inflationary pressure. Electricity is just going very high. And this company uses 45 gigawatts of power in here.

headline: Sharesies sees 10–15 deceased estates per week on platform, highlighting widespread lack of estate planning among retail investors
reasoning: Naomi Gary notes that despite having over one million customers, 70% of survey respondents lacked a will. The platform processes 10–15 deceased estates per week, and research suggests widows — particularly younger ones — face elevated risk of falling below the poverty line without proper estate planning in place.
quote: We've got over a million customers on the platform now. And we've got a really diverse range of customers, about 65% of our customers are under the age of 40. But we still see 10, 15 deceased estates a week.
episode_title: Are you leaving your wealth in limbo?

headline: Professional executor fee models warrant scrutiny as some organisations charge up to 8% of estate value under 'free will' schemes
reasoning: Tammy McLeod warns that some organisations offer free wills but recoup costs through large executor fees — potentially 8% of the entire estate value — effectively making them very expensive for beneficiaries. She contrasts this with transparent upfront fee models, noting that lay executors cannot charge fees under New Zealand law.
quote: There are other organizations which do charge large fees, and we're seeing some of that in the press at the moment... hey, we're leaving you the house, it's, oh, actually we're going to have to sell the house because somebody needs to take 8% of the entire value of someone's wealth.
episode_title: Are you leaving your wealth in limbo?
